abstract: |
  This report builds a model of where people living in HDB flats board the train on a
  weekday morning, and uses it to ask what the planned Jurong Region Line (JRL) and Cross
  Island Line (CRL) would change.

  The model is a Huff model. It shares the 1.18 million dwelling units of 10,817 HDB
  blocks among the stations around each block, giving more to stations that are closer
  and to stations that are more attractive. It is calibrated against three months of LTA
  tap-in counts (August to October 2026) at the 148 stations that have HDB homes around
  them.

  Tested on stations it was not fitted to, the model ranks stations well (rank correlation
  0.90) but its estimate for any single station is typically about a third off. Stations
  that serve more lines, and stations with more shops and services around them, are
  associated with more boardings; stations served only by LRT with far fewer.

  In the network the brief asks about (today's plus the JRL and CRL phase 1), the new
  stations with the most HDB homes around them, Tengah Plantation, Serangoon North and
  Pasir Ris East, have the largest modelled morning boardings. Several JRL and CRL
  stations in industrial, university and airport areas have almost none; this says that
  few HDB residents live near them, not that nobody will use them. Because the model holds
  the number of homes fixed, the new lines redistribute boardings rather than add them:
  Chinese Garden, Lakeside and Pioneer lose the most.

  As a value-added analysis, I let the effect of distance differ by region. Residents of
  the North-East and West appear about twice as sensitive to distance as those in the
  Central region; the regional model predicts held-out stations better, and the main
  conclusions hold under it.

# Why this matters

Singapore plans its rail network years ahead of the people who will ride it. LTA
builds some stations as shells and opens them when the riders arrive, and sometimes
they arrive late. Hume station on the Downtown Line was finished in 2015 and opened on
28 February 2025. Buangkok and Woodleigh stayed closed when the North East Line opened
in 2003, because too few people were expected to use them. Deciding when a station
opens, and how a new line will change the stations around it, needs an estimate of
demand before anyone has used the station.

This exercise builds that estimate for the two lines under construction: the Jurong
Region Line in the west, and phase 1 of the Cross Island Line from Aviation Park to
Bright Hill.

A station's catchment is not a hard boundary. A block of flats between two stations
belongs to neither: some of its residents walk to one and some to the other, depending
on how far each is and what each offers. A Huff model describes exactly that, which is
why it is the method used here.

# Research question and objectives

**Where do HDB residents board the train in the weekday morning peak, and how would
the planned JRL and CRL stations change that?**

The brief sets three objectives. @tbl-brief shows where each of its tasks is answered.

1. Calibrate a probabilistic spatial interaction (Huff) model that estimates
   morning boardings at each station from where people live, how far each station is,
   and what each station offers.
2. Use it to predict morning boardings at the planned JRL and CRL stations.
3. Show how the new stations would change the boardings and catchments of the stations
   already open.

| Task in the brief | Where it is done |
|---|---|
| Spatial interaction data frame for the existing network | `si_existing`, section 4.5 |
| Spatial interaction data frame with the proposed stations | `si_2030`, section 4.5; phased variants in 7.1 |
| Origin table with local market potential | `origins` (HDB dwelling units), section 4.1 |
| Destination table with observed ridership and attraction variables | `stations`, sections 4.2 to 4.4 |
| Calibrate a probabilistic spatial interaction model | sections 5 and 6 |
| Estimate ridership at existing stations, with graphics and maps | section 6 |
| Predict ridership at existing and proposed stations | section 7 |
| Show the impact on the market areas of existing stations | sections 7.3 and 7.4 |

# Data and study design

## What exactly is being modelled

The brief asks for station-level ridership. This report models one well-defined part
of it, and it is worth being precise about what that part is.

- **Boardings** are tap-ins: people entering a station through the fare gates.
- **The time window** is weekday mornings, 06:00 to 09:00, averaged over August,
  September and October 2026. Values are boardings per month in that window.
- **Riders come from home.** In the morning most trips start at home, so the people
  boarding at a station mostly live near it. That is the assumption a residential
  catchment model needs. Later in the day it fails: a central-area station boards
  thousands of people in the evening who live nowhere near it (@fig-inout).
- **Homes are HDB flats.** The number of HDB dwelling units in each block is the
  "local market potential". HDB flats house about four in five Singapore residents, and
  they are the only homes with a public, block-level count. Private housing is not
  included, which matters (section 4.3).
- **A station is one place.** An interchange such as Jurong East counts once, whatever
  the number of lines it serves.

@tbl-kinds separates what is measured from what is assumed, because the conclusions
depend on the difference.

| Kind | Items |
|---|---|
| Observed | Tap-ins per station (LTA); HDB dwelling units and block locations; station locations; bus stops and points of interest (OpenStreetMap) |
| Proxy | Dwelling units for the number of people who might board; straight-line distance for the journey to the station; counts of nearby places for a station's appeal |
| Estimated | The distance-decay exponent, the attraction exponents and the trip rate *k* |
| Predicted | Boardings at new stations, and changes at existing ones |
| Assumed | Homes and surroundings stay as they are today; riders choose only among stations within 3 km; total morning demand from HDB homes does not change when stations are added |

: What is measured, what stands in for something else, and what is assumed. {#tbl-kinds}

The brief recommends the origin-destination version of the passenger data. On the day
I ran the analysis, DataMall refused that endpoint for my account with a quota error,
while the station-level endpoint worked. For a model of where people *board*, the
station-level counts are all that is needed: where each trip ends plays no part in it.
LTA's bus stop file also could not be downloaded by script, so OpenStreetMap supplies
the bus stops (5,668 of them).

# Data preparation and quality checks

Every check quoted in this section is computed in `R/04b_diagnostics.R`.

## Placing every HDB block

The number of homes and the building outlines come in two files with no shared key.
The property file names a block by number and a shortened street name ("1 BEDOK STH AVE
1"); the building file by number, a street code ("BEA09N") and a postal code. Matching
on block number alone is wrong, because the same block number appears in many towns.

The street code turned out to be one code per street (657 street names, 660 codes). So
I looked up one block per street in OneMap, Singapore's official address search, and
matched the postal code it returned to a building outline. That gives a complete
street-to-code lookup (`R/01_street_codes.R`), and with it 10,734 of the 10,817
residential blocks join to their outline. The remaining 83, mostly new Tengah blocks
that are not yet in the building file, were looked up one by one and kept as points.

The checks: no block was matched to two outlines
(`r D$origins_dup_postal` duplicates), no two blocks share a location
(`r D$origins_same_xy`), no geometry is empty (`r D$origins_empty_geom`), and the total
of `r num(D$origins_du_total)` dwelling units equals the total in the property file. All
distances are measured in metres in SVY21 (EPSG:3414). Each block is represented by a
point inside its outline (`st_point_on_surface()`), which, unlike a centroid, cannot fall
outside an L-shaped block.

```{r fig-origins}
#| fig-cap: "The local market potential: 10,817 HDB residential blocks, sized by dwelling units, with today's stations and the 29 new JRL and CRL phase 1 stations."
#| fig-height: 5.6
s_all <- lines_sf(stations)
ggplot() + base_land(subzone) +
  geom_sf(data = origins, aes(size = du), colour = PAL$muted, alpha = 0.25, stroke = 0) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(s_all, kind == "Existing"), shape = 21, fill = "white", colour = PAL$ink, size = 1.1, stroke = 0.4) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(s_all, kind != "Existing"), aes(fill = kind), shape = 21, colour = "white", size = 2.3, stroke = 0.4) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 1.6, guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Jurong Region Line" = LINE_COLS[["JRL"]], "Cross Island Line" = LINE_COLS[["CRL"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(caption = "Sources: HDB Property Information and Existing Building (data.gov.sg); station coordinates from URA via data.gov.sg.") +
  sg_crop(stations) + theme_map()
```

## Stations and the passenger data

The passenger data decides which stations exist, not any station list. Three traps had
to be cleared.

- **Stations listed as planned that are already open.** Keppel, Cantonment and Prince
  Edward Road (Circle Line stage 6, opened on 12 July 2026) are listed as future stations
  but carry passengers in all three months. They are moved to today's network, together with the new Circle Line
  codes at Marina Bay (CC33) and Bayfront (CC34).
- **Stations that are built but not open.** LTA's own September 2026 station layer
  contains platforms at Bukit Brown, Mount Pleasant, Marina South and Founders' Memorial,
  and a dozen depots, none of which board a passenger. Using that layer as the network
  would have added exactly the kind of unopened station the brief describes.
- **Joint codes.** The passenger data records an interchange under one combined code
  ("NS27/CC33/TE20"), and in one case (Stevens) under two separate codes. Each code is
  mapped to its station, and all `r D$pv_codes_total` codes are used once.

Station locations agree with LTA's station outlines: for the `r D$coord_summary$n` codes in
both, the median distance is `r round(D$coord_summary$median_m)` m and the largest
`r round(D$coord_summary$max_m)` m. Morning boardings are stable from month to month (the
correlation of log tap-ins between August and October is `r round(mon_cor[1, 3], 3)`), so
averaging the three months loses little.

## Which stations the model is fitted to

`r sum(ex$du_1km < CAL_MIN_DU_1KM)` stations have fewer than 1,000 HDB dwelling units within
1 km. Some serve private estates (Newton, Stevens, Sixth Avenue, Siglap), some industry
(the four Tuas stations, Joo Koon), the airport or the central area. Newton and Kranji
each board over 200,000 people a month in the morning with no HDB block within a
kilometre. A model whose only source of riders is HDB flats cannot explain them.

So these stations stay in every block's choice set, where they compete for HDB riders
like any other station, but their observed boardings are not used to fit the model. The
data support the rule (@fig-inout): the `r n_fit` fitted stations board
`r round(with(st_drop_geometry(stn)[ci, ], sum(tap_am) / sum(tapout_am)), 2)` morning tap-ins for
every tap-out; the excluded ones only
`r round(with(st_drop_geometry(stn)[-ci, ], sum(tap_am) / sum(tapout_am)), 2)`.

The rule is a trade-off, and section 9 measures it. Dropping it entirely, so that the
model must also explain private-estate, central and industrial stations, makes it worse
at the residential stations it can explain and changes its predictions for the new
stations by `r pct(sens$sens$new_total_vs_main[1] - 1)`. Setting the threshold at 500 or 2,000
instead of 1,000 changes little.

## Attraction variables

Each station's attractiveness is described by four things counted within 400 m, about a
five-minute walk:

- **lines served** (today's for calibration, the planned network's for prediction);
- **bus stops**, as a measure of feeder connections;
- **points of interest**: shops, food outlets, offices, schools, clinics and civic
  amenities in OpenStreetMap (mapped areas such as malls are reduced to one point each);
- **LRT-only**: whether the station is served only by a light rail line.

Counts enter as log(1 + count). The four variables are not strongly related to each
other: the largest correlation is `r round(max(abs(D$cor_X[upper.tri(D$cor_X)])), 2)` and every variance
inflation factor is below `r ceiling(max(D$vif) * 10) / 10`, so their effects can be estimated
separately.

## The two spatial interaction data frames

The model works on a table with one row for each block and each station it could
reasonably use. A block's choice set is every station within 3 km, plus its three
nearest stations if fewer are that close, so that blocks far from the network (Tengah has
no station today) still have a choice. The median block has ten candidate stations.
Distances under 100 m are set to 100 m, so that a block next to a station does not get an
infinitely strong pull.

```{r tbl-si}
#| tbl-cap: "The size of the two spatial interaction data frames, and their first rows. `si_2030` adds the JRL and CRL phase 1 stations to each block's choice set."
si_now <- read_rds(file.path(DER, "si_existing.rds")); si_30 <- read_rds(file.path(DER, "si_2030.rds"))
tibble(table = c("si_existing", "si_2030"), rows = c(nrow(si_now), nrow(si_30)),
       origins = c(n_distinct(si_now$origin_id), n_distinct(si_30$origin_id)),
       destinations = c(n_distinct(si_now$name), n_distinct(si_30$name)),
       `median choices per block` = c(median(table(si_now$origin_id)), median(table(si_30$origin_id)))) |>
  kable(format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
head(si_30 |> mutate(dist = round(dist)), 4) |> kable()
```

# The model

## How the Huff model shares out each block's residents

The probability that a resident of block $i$ boards at station $j$ is

$$
P_{ij} = \frac{A_j \, d_{ij}^{\lambda}}{\sum_{l \in C_i} A_l \, d_{il}^{\lambda}},
\qquad
A_j = \exp\Big(\sum_m \gamma_m x_{jm}\Big)
$$

In words: each candidate station gets a score that rises with its attractiveness $A_j$ and
falls with distance $d_{ij}$ (in metres; $\lambda$ is negative), and the block's residents
are shared in proportion to the scores. $C_i$ is the block's choice set. Attractiveness
multiplies together the effects of the station's characteristics $x_{jm}$, which is the
form of attractiveness used in an MCI model; with one distance term, the model as a whole
is a Huff model.

The predicted boardings at a station are the homes it draws, times one trip rate $k$:

$$
\hat T_j = k \sum_i DU_i \, P_{ij}
$$

The fitted $k$ is `r round(D$k, 1)` morning boardings per dwelling unit per month, about
`r round(D$k_per_weekday, 2)` per weekday. It is a single number for every block, so it
assumes that every HDB home produces the same number of morning trips.

@fig-example shows what the model does for one block in Tengah.

```{r fig-example}
#| fig-cap: "The model applied to one block (220A Tengah Garden Walk, 188 flats). Each bar is the share of its residents expected to board at that station. Today they are spread across four distant stations; with the JRL, two new stations near the block take most of them."
#| fig-height: 3.4
eg <- "220A | TENGAH GDN WALK"
d <- bind_rows(scn$sh_now |> filter(origin_id == eg) |> mutate(network = "Today"),
               scn$sh_30 |> filter(origin_id == eg) |> mutate(network = "With JRL and CRL phase 1")) |>
  group_by(network) |> slice_max(p, n = 5) |> ungroup() |>
  mutate(new = name %in% newS$name)
ggplot(d, aes(p, reorder(name, p), fill = new)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = pct(p)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3, colour = PAL$ink) +
  facet_wrap(~network, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = PAL$accent_lt, `TRUE` = LINE_COLS[["JRL"]]),
                    labels = c(`FALSE` = "Existing station", `TRUE` = "New JRL station"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25))) +
  labs(x = "Share of the block's residents", y = NULL) + theme_ex03(grid = "x")
```

## Calibration

The unknowns, $\lambda$ and the $\gamma_m$, are chosen so that predicted boardings match
observed boardings as closely as possible on the log scale, across the fitted stations.
Boardings range from under a thousand to over 400,000 a month; on the log scale a 20%
miss counts the same at a small station as at a large one. For any choice of the
unknowns, the best $k$ can be worked out directly, so the optimiser does not have to
search for it.

Because the score inside the model is a sum of terms each multiplied by one unknown, the
model is mathematically a conditional logit, and the error has an exact gradient
(`R/huff_core.R`). That made each fit take about two seconds, which is what makes the
cross-validation and bootstrap below practical. Every fit converged.

The shares were checked against `MCI::huff.shares()`, the course's reference
implementation: for one block they agree to the 15th decimal place (largest difference
`r sprintf("%.1e", cal$mci_check)`). I wrote my own version only because MCI requires every
block to have the same set of candidate stations, which a 3 km choice set does not give.

```{r code-core}
#| code-summary: "R/huff_core.R: the model, its error and its gradient"
```

## How the model is tested

Four versions of the model are compared, from simple to full:

| Model | What makes a station attractive | Distance exponent |
|---|---|---|
| M0 | nothing: every station equal | -2, the textbook default, not fitted |
| M1 | nothing | fitted |
| M2 | lines served | fitted |
| M3 | lines, bus stops, points of interest, LRT-only | fitted |

: The four models. {#tbl-models}

Each is scored by **10-fold cross-validation over stations**: the 148 stations are split
into ten groups; each group in turn has its ridership hidden, the model is fitted on the
other nine, and the hidden stations are predicted. Hidden stations stay in every choice
set, so they still compete for riders; only their ridership is hidden. Everything learned
from ridership, the exponents and $k$, is learned from the nine training groups only.
Nothing else depends on ridership, so no information leaks from the hidden stations into
the fit.

This tests the right thing for a new station, whose location and surroundings are known
and whose ridership is not. It is still not a test of a real opening, for two reasons.
The hidden stations are mature, with established riding habits; a new station starts
from nothing and builds up. And homes and surroundings are fixed at today's. A true test
would fit the model to data from before a station opened and compare it with ridership
after. DataMall only provides the latest three months, so that cannot be done here. The
three Circle Line stage 6 stations show why it matters: their morning boardings are still
rising month to month, by `r pct(with(D$ccl6 |> filter(pt_code == "CC32"), tap_am[YEAR_MONTH == "2026-10"] / tap_am[YEAR_MONTH == "2026-08"] - 1))`
at Prince Edward Road between August and October.

# Calibration results

## Accuracy: good at ranking stations, rougher on any one station

```{r tbl-fit}
#| tbl-cap: "Cross-validated accuracy on the 148 fitted stations, all models scored on the same ten groups. R² is on log boardings. MAE and RMSE are in boardings per month. WAPE is the total absolute error as a share of total boardings; bias is the error in the total; MdAPE is the typical (median) percentage error for one station."
cmp |> filter(model %in% c("M0", "M1", "M2", "M3")) |>
  transmute(Model = model, `R² (log)` = round(R2_log, 2), MAE = num(MAE, 100), RMSE = num(RMSE, 100),
            `WAPE %` = round(WAPE_pct), `Bias %` = round(bias_pct), `MdAPE %` = round(MdAPE_pct),
            `Rank correlation` = round(spearman, 2)) |>
  kable()
```

The textbook model already explains `r pct(m_of("M0", "R2_log"))` of the variation in log
boardings: where the homes are does much of the work. Fitting the distance exponent alone
adds nothing. Adding the number of lines raises it to `r pct(m_of("M2", "R2_log"))`, and the
full model to `r pct(m_of("M3", "R2_log"))`.

In plain terms, the full model puts stations in nearly the right order (rank correlation
`r round(m_of("M3", "spearman"), 2)`), but its estimate for any one station is typically
`r round(m_of("M3", "MdAPE_pct"))`% off, and the absolute errors add up to
`r round(m_of("M3", "WAPE_pct"))`% of all boardings. Its total for the fitted stations is
`r round(m_of("M3", "bias_pct"))`% too high: the model is fitted on the log scale, which
weighs every station equally rather than every boarding.

A high R² for existing stations does not by itself mean the model will predict new
stations well. The cross-validation is the closer test, and section 5.3 explains what
even that cannot test.

```{r fig-obs-pred}
#| fig-cap: "Observed against predicted morning boardings for the 148 fitted stations, each predicted while its own ridership was hidden. Points on the dashed line are exact; the dotted lines mark a factor of two. Labelled: the ten largest misses."
#| fig-height: 5.4
d <- st_drop_geometry(stn)[ci, ] |> mutate(cv = cvp[ci], err = log(tap_am / cv))
lab <- d |> slice_max(abs(err), n = 10)
ggplot(d, aes(cv, tap_am)) +
  geom_abline(colour = PAL$muted, linewidth = 0.3, linetype = 2) +
  geom_abline(intercept = log10(2), colour = PAL$muted, linewidth = 0.2, linetype = 3) +
  geom_abline(intercept = -log10(2), colour = PAL$muted, linewidth = 0.2, linetype = 3) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = lrt_only), size = 1.9, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text_repel(data = lab, aes(label = name), size = 2.8, colour = PAL$ink, seed = 2, min.segment.length = 0) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) + scale_y_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = PAL$accent, `TRUE` = LINE_COLS[["LRT"]]),
                      labels = c(`FALSE` = "MRT", `TRUE` = "LRT only"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Predicted boardings per month (log scale)", y = "Observed tap-ins, weekdays 06:00 to 09:00, per month (log scale)") +
  theme_ex03(grid = "both")
```

## What makes a station attractive

```{r fig-params}
#| fig-cap: "Estimated exponents of the full model (M3), with 95% intervals from 200 bootstrap refits that resample the fitted stations. Positive values mean more attractive."
#| fig-height: 3.2
lab_terms <- c(lambda = "Distance exponent", n_lines = "Lines served", bus_stops = "Bus stops within 400 m",
               poi = "Points of interest within 400 m", lrt_only = "LRT-only station")
p <- tibble(term = names(th), estimate = th) |> left_join(cal$ci, by = "term") |>
  mutate(term = factor(lab_terms[term], rev(lab_terms)))
ggplot(p, aes(estimate, term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = PAL$muted, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0, colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL$accent, size = 2.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", estimate)), vjust = -0.9, size = 3, colour = PAL$ink) +
  labs(x = "Estimate (exponent on log(1 + count), or coefficient on the LRT indicator)", y = NULL) +
  theme_ex03(grid = "x")
```

Turned into multipliers, and holding the other variables fixed:

- **Lines served.** A station with two lines is estimated to be
  `r round((3/2)^th[["n_lines"]], 1)` times as attractive as one with one line. Saving a
  transfer is a plausible reason, but the model only shows the association; it cannot
  separate the effect of the extra line from everything else that tends to come with
  interchanges.
- **Points of interest.** Ten times as many shops and services around a station goes
  with about `r round(10^th[["poi"]], 1)` times the attractiveness.
- **LRT-only.** An LRT-only station has about `r pct(exp(th[["lrt_only"]]))` of the
  attractiveness of an MRT station with the same characteristics. Part of this is how
  the data count LRT riders: a Punggol resident who boards the LRT and changes to the
  North East Line taps in only once.
- **Distance.** Doubling the distance to a station cuts its pull by a factor of about
  `r round(2^-th[["lambda"]], 1)` (exponent `r round(th[["lambda"]], 2)`).
- **Bus stops.** Once the other variables are in the model, the number of bus stops adds
  nothing that can be distinguished from zero: its interval spans zero.

One caution about reading these numbers separately. In the bootstrap, the distance
exponent and the LRT effect move together (correlation
`r round(D$boot_cor["lambda", "lrt_only"], 2)`): LRT stops sit very close to the blocks they
serve, so the data cannot fully tell "LRT stations are less attractive" apart from
"distance matters more". Their combined effect is well determined; the split between
them is not.

## Where the model misses

```{r fig-resid-map}
#| fig-cap: "Prediction error at each fitted station: log of observed over predicted. Teal: more boardings than the model expects; red: fewer."
#| fig-height: 5
d <- stn[ci, ]
ggplot() + base_land(subzone) +
  geom_sf(data = d, aes(fill = pmax(pmin(resid_log, 1.2), -1.2)), shape = 21, size = 2.4, colour = "white", stroke = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$div, limits = c(-1.2, 1.2), name = "log(observed / predicted)") +
  sg_crop(stations) + theme_map()
```

The errors are not scattered at random: stations near each other tend to be wrong in the
same direction. Moran's I of the errors is `r round(D$moran_perm$statistic, 2)` with each
station's six nearest neighbours (p = `r D$moran_perm$p.value` in a 999-run permutation test),
and it stays significant with 4, 8 or 10 neighbours (I between
`r round(min(D$moran_k$I), 2)` and `r round(max(D$moran_k$I), 2)`).

The largest under-predictions are city-fringe stations where HDB blocks sit among
condominiums and landed homes: Novena, Great World, Katong Park, Fort Canning, Beauty
World, Aljunied. The largest over-predictions are stations that opened recently (Keppel)
and stations whose blocks mostly use a neighbouring station instead (Bendemeer, Labrador
Park, one-north). These are explanations consistent with where the errors fall, not
proven causes: the model has no data on private homes or on how long a station has been
open. Section 8 tests one explanation that can be tested, that distance matters
differently in different parts of Singapore.

```{r code-04}

#| code-summary: "R/04_calibrate.R and R/04b_diagnostics.R: calibration, validation and checks"

```

# Predictions for the expanded network

## Which network

The brief asks for today's network compared with today's network plus the JRL and the
CRL phase 1, and describes that as the network by 2030. That comparison is the main one in
this report and the slides. Whether it is literally the 2030 network depends on LTA's
current schedules, which are recorded with their sources in
`future_station_schedule.csv` and used to build two further networks (`R/05b_phased_scenarios.R`):

```{r tbl-phased}
#| tbl-cap: "The three networks compared. All hold today's homes and surroundings fixed, so they show where today's HDB residents would board on each network, not ridership in a given year."
lab_scn <- c(brief = "Brief: today + JRL + CRL phase 1", end_2030 = "End of 2030, by LTA's current schedules",
             full = "Every planned station in the station list")
ph$summary |> mutate(Network = lab_scn[scenario]) |>
  transmute(Network, Stations = stations, `New stations` = new_stations,
            `Boardings at new stations, per month` = num(new_boardings, 1000)) |>
  kable()
```

```{r phase-numbers}
#| include: false
jc <- res$name[res$new]
pb <- ph$runs |> filter(scenario == "brief", name %in% jc) |> select(name, brief = pred)
pe <- ph$runs |> filter(scenario == "end_2030", name %in% jc) |> select(name, e2030 = pred)
pp <- inner_join(pb, pe, by = "name")
rho_be <- cor(pp$brief, pp$e2030, method = "spearman")
tot_be <- sum(pp$e2030) / sum(pp$brief) - 1
east <- ph$runs |> filter(scenario %in% c("brief", "end_2030"), !new) |>
  select(name, scenario, pred) |> pivot_wider(names_from = scenario, values_from = pred) |>
  mutate(d = end_2030 / brief - 1) |> arrange(d)
```

LTA's published schedules, checked on 14 November 2026, put the JRL's three stages in
2028 and 2029 (LTA says the dates for stages 2 and 3 will be updated) and the CRL phase 1
by 2030. So the brief's network matches the official plan for the end of 2030, with
two corrections.

- **JS2A is not part of it.** The station list includes JS2A (between Choa Chu Kang West
  and Tengah), an infill station LTA announced in March 2026 and plans to open in the
  mid-2030s, when the area around it is developed. It is not one of the JRL's 24 stations,
  and the brief's network here leaves it out. (The station list calls it "Forest Hill"; LTA
  has not published a name.)
- **Other lines also open before 2030.** Bedok South, Sungei Bedok and Xilin open on
  26 December 2026, and Founders' Memorial is to open with the memorial, which is due at
  the end of 2028 (the year is inferred from the memorial's schedule, not stated by LTA).
  They are in the end-2030 network but not in the brief's.

Adding those four stations hardly affects the JRL and CRL results: the new stations'
ranking is unchanged (rank correlation `r sprintf("%.2f", rho_be)`) and their total changes by
`r if (abs(tot_be) < 0.001) "less than 0.1%" else pct(tot_be, 0.1)`. The extra stations are in the east, far from both lines; the existing
station most affected by them is `r east$name[1]` (`r pct(east$d[1])`). So the brief's
comparison is a fair stand-in for the end-2030 network for this question. The full planned
network, which also adds the CRL phase 2 and Punggol extension (2032), Brickland (2034),
Sungei Kadut (2035), the Changi Terminal 5 stations (mid-2030s) and stations with no
announced date, is shown in @tbl-phased only for completeness: it is not a forecast of any
particular year.

## Morning boardings at the new stations

```{r fig-new}
#| fig-cap: "Modelled weekday morning boardings per month from HDB homes at the 29 new JRL and CRL phase 1 stations. Bars show 95% intervals for parameter uncertainty only (section 9). The grey band is today's fitted stations between their 10th and 50th percentiles."
#| fig-height: 7
q <- quantile(stn$tap_am[ci], c(0.1, 0.5))
d <- res |> filter(new) |> mutate(name = reorder(name, pred_2030),
                                 line = ifelse(line_new == "JRL", "Jurong Region Line", "Cross Island Line"))
ggplot(d, aes(pred_2030, name)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = q[1], xmax = q[2], ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = PAL$land, alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = pred_2030_lo, xmax = pred_2030_hi, colour = line), height = 0, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = line), size = 2.2) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Jurong Region Line" = LINE_COLS[["JRL"]], "Cross Island Line" = LINE_COLS[["CRL"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Modelled boardings per month from HDB homes, weekdays 06:00 to 09:00 (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_ex03(grid = "x")
```

```{r new-numbers}
#| include: false
nn <- res |> filter(new) |> arrange(-pred_2030)
low <- nn |> filter(pred_2030 < q[1])
tg <- apply(units::drop_units(st_distance(filter(origins, PLN_AREA_N == "TENGAH"), ex)), 1, min) / 1000
tg_min <- round(min(tg), 1); tg_max <- round(max(tg), 1); tg_med <- round(median(tg), 1)
```

The new stations with the most modelled morning boardings are those placed among HDB
blocks that have no station of their own today. Tengah Plantation
(`r num(nn$pred_2030[nn$name == "Tengah Plantation"], 1000)` a month) is the clearest case:
Tengah's `r num(sum(origins$du[origins$PLN_AREA_N == "TENGAH"]))` dwelling units are
`r tg_min` to `r tg_max` km (median `r tg_med` km) in a straight line from the nearest station
today. On the CRL, Serangoon North
(`r num(nn$pred_2030[nn$name == "Serangoon North"], 1000)`) and Pasir Ris East
(`r num(nn$pred_2030[nn$name == "Pasir Ris East"], 1000)`) serve large estates between
today's lines.

`r nrow(low)` new stations fall below the 10th percentile of today's fitted stations:
`r paste(as.character(low$name), collapse = ", ")`. Most are in the Jurong Innovation
District, at the university or near the airport. **This shows that few HDB residents live
near them; it does not show that they will be little used.** They are built for jobs,
campuses and the airport, and that demand would appear as people arriving in the morning
(tap-outs), which this model does not estimate. Their surroundings will also change by the
time they open, in either direction, so today's figure is neither a floor nor a ceiling.

## How the new lines redistribute boardings at existing stations

The model holds the number of homes and the trip rate fixed, so adding stations cannot
add boardings: the total predicted morning boardings are the same in both networks (the
difference is `r signif(D$conservation$diff_pct, 1)`%). What changes is where people board.
So every change below is a **reallocation of modelled HDB-origin morning boardings**.

```{r fig-change-bars}
#| fig-cap: "Change in modelled morning boardings at existing stations when the JRL and CRL phase 1 are added: the 15 largest losses and every gain. Labels give the percentage change."
#| fig-height: 5.6
d <- res |> filter(existing, !is.na(change)) |>
  filter(rank(change) <= 15 | change > 0) |>
  mutate(name = reorder(name, change), dir = ifelse(change > 0, "gain", "loss"))
ggplot(d, aes(change, name, fill = dir)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = pct(change_pct), hjust = ifelse(change > 0, -0.15, 1.15)), size = 2.9, colour = PAL$ink) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(gain = PAL$accent, loss = PAL$loss), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.18, 0.18))) +
  labs(x = "Change in modelled boardings per month, weekdays 06:00 to 09:00", y = NULL) +
  theme_ex03(grid = "x")
```

```{r fig-impact}
#| fig-cap: "Where the changes fall: percentage change in modelled morning boardings at existing stations (circle size: today's modelled boardings). New stations in their line colours."
#| fig-height: 5.6
d <- stations |> select(name) |> left_join(res, by = "name")
ggplot() + base_land(subzone) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(d, existing, !is.na(change_pct)),
          aes(fill = pmin(pmax(change_pct, -0.6), 0.3), size = pred_now), shape = 21, colour = "white", stroke = 0.25) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(d, new), aes(colour = line_new), shape = 18, size = 2.4) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c(PAL$loss, "#D88C74", PAL$loss_lt, "#B9BEC6", PAL$accent), values = rescale(c(-0.6, -0.3, -0.1, 0, 0.3)),
                       limits = c(-0.6, 0.3), labels = label_percent(), name = "Change") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(JRL = LINE_COLS[["JRL"]], CRL = LINE_COLS[["CRL"]]), name = "New station") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 5, guide = "none") +
  sg_crop(stations) + theme_map()
```

The losses fall where the new lines run between existing stations rather than beyond
them. In the west, the JRL's Jurong West branch takes blocks that today use Chinese
Garden, Lakeside, Pioneer and Boon Lay, and the Tengah stations take blocks from Bukit
Batok and Bukit Gombak. In the north-east, Serangoon North and Tavistock take blocks from
Kovan and Serangoon. The only stations that gain are the four that become Cross Island
Line interchanges: Hougang, Bright Hill, Ang Mo Kio and Pasir Ris.

What these numbers do not say is as important. Fewer people entering Lakeside does not
mean emptier trains past Lakeside: many residents who now board the JRL will still change
to the East-West Line at Jurong East or Boon Lay. Train loads depend on the routes people
take and on train capacity, which this model does not represent. The changes describe
station access (where people enter the network), not crowding.

## How catchments change

```{r fig-market}
#| fig-cap: "Catchments in the west. Left: each HDB block coloured by the station that draws the largest share of its residents today. Right: the blocks whose main station changes when the JRL is added, and whether they move to a new station or to another existing one. Same extent and projection (SVY21) in both panels."
#| fig-height: 5.4
west <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(c(xmin = 11000, xmax = 23500, ymin = 31000, ymax = 42500), crs = st_crs(STUDY_CRS)))
o_w <- origins |> st_filter(west) |> left_join(scn$dom, by = "origin_id")
top <- union(names(sort(table(o_w$station_now), decreasing = TRUE))[1:12], names(sort(table(o_w$station_2030), decreasing = TRUE))[1:14])
pal_st <- setNames(rep_len(c("#137C8B", "#B4432F", "#5E7CA4", "#C9913D", "#4E8F5A", "#8A5A8C", "#2F6F86", "#C76B4F",
                             "#7A8F3C", "#9C6B3F", "#3E7F72", "#A2546C", "#5C6C99", "#B08A2E", "#6F5A9A", "#3F8A5C"), length(top)), top)
stn_w <- st_filter(lines_sf(stations), west)
o_w <- o_w |> mutate(change = case_when(to_new ~ "Switches to a new station",
                                       switched ~ "Switches to another existing station",
                                       TRUE ~ "Keeps its station"))
p_now <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = st_crop(subzone, west), fill = PAL$land, colour = PAL$land_line, linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = o_w, aes(colour = ifelse(station_now %in% top, station_now, "other")), size = 0.7) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(stn_w, existing), shape = 21, size = 1.8, colour = PAL$ink, fill = "white") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal_st, other = PAL$null), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Today") + theme_map() + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 11))
p_30 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = st_crop(subzone, west), fill = PAL$land, colour = PAL$land_line, linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = o_w, aes(colour = change), size = 0.7) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(stn_w, existing), shape = 21, size = 1.8, colour = PAL$ink, fill = "white") +
  geom_sf(data = filter(stn_w, !existing), aes(fill = kind), shape = 23, size = 2.4, colour = PAL$ink) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Switches to a new station" = LINE_COLS[["JRL"]],
                                 "Switches to another existing station" = PAL$loss,
                                 "Keeps its station" = PAL$null), name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Jurong Region Line" = LINE_COLS[["JRL"]], "Cross Island Line" = LINE_COLS[["CRL"]]), guide = "none") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2, override.aes = list(size = 3))) +
  labs(title = "With the JRL and CRL phase 1") + theme_map() + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 11))
(p_now + p_30) & theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = NA))
```

Across Singapore, `r num(sum(scn$dom$switched))` of the 10,817 blocks change their main
station, `r num(sum(scn$dom$to_new))` of them to a new one. The west changes most: Tengah's
blocks, which today sit at the edge of several catchments, get stations of their own, and
the Jurong West estates divide among four JRL stations.

```{r code-05}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "R/05_scenario.R and R/05b_phased_scenarios.R: the expanded networks"
```

# Value-added analysis: does distance matter equally everywhere?

```{r va-numbers}
#| include: false
lr <- va$lambda_region |> mutate(region = str_to_title(sub(" REGION", "", region)))
lrv <- function(r, col = "lambda", a = 1) round(lr[[col]][lr$region == r], a)
```

The full model uses one distance exponent for the whole island, and its errors cluster in
space. That is the same assumption that geographically weighted regression relaxes in
Lessons 9 and 10: one number says that a resident of Punggol and a resident of Bukit Merah
weigh distance against station quality in the same way. Estates are laid out differently,
and feeder services differ, so the effect of distance may differ too. This is a question
about geography, and it can be tested.

I fitted two extensions of M3 and scored them with the same ten cross-validation groups:

- **R5**: one distance exponent for each of the five regions, according to where the
  home block is;
- **EXP**: an exponential rather than a power distance decay, the usual alternative form.

```{r fig-va}
#| fig-cap: "Left: distance exponent by region of the home block, with 95% bootstrap intervals (100 refits); the dashed line is the island-wide exponent. Right: cross-validated accuracy (R² of log boardings) of the three model forms."
#| fig-height: 3.6
cv_va <- cmp |> filter(model %in% c("M3", "R5", "EXP")) |>
  mutate(model = recode(model, M3 = "M3: one exponent", R5 = "R5: exponent per region", EXP = "EXP: exponential decay"))
p1 <- ggplot(lr, aes(lambda, reorder(region, lambda))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = th[["lambda"]], linetype = 2, colour = PAL$muted, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0, colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL$accent, size = 2.4) +
  labs(x = "Distance exponent", y = NULL) + theme_ex03(grid = "x")
p2 <- ggplot(cv_va, aes(R2_log, reorder(model, R2_log))) +
  geom_col(fill = PAL$accent_lt, width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", R2_log)), hjust = 1.1, size = 3, colour = PAL$ink) +
  labs(x = "Cross-validated R² (log boardings)", y = NULL) + theme_ex03(grid = "x")
p1 + p2 + plot_layout(widths = c(1.1, 1))
```

**Distance matters more in the North-East and West.** The exponent is
`r lrv("North-East", a = 2)` for homes in the North-East (interval `r lrv("North-East", "lo")` to
`r lrv("North-East", "hi")`) and `r lrv("West", a = 2)` in the West (`r lrv("West", "lo")` to
`r lrv("West", "hi")`), against `r lrv("Central", a = 2)` in the Central region
(`r lrv("Central", "lo")` to `r lrv("Central", "hi")`). The Central interval barely overlaps the
other two. A plausible reading is that in towns such as Sengkang, Punggol, Jurong West and
Choa Chu Kang each neighbourhood is laid out around its own MRT or LRT stop, so residents
use the nearest; in Toa Payoh, Bishan or Queenstown several stations are within a short
walk and residents are freer to pass the nearest. The model shows the difference, not the
reason.

**The North and East exponents cannot be pinned down.** Their intervals span almost any
plausible value. Blocks in the North reach only 11 stations within their choice sets, and
only 9 Northern and 13 Eastern stations are in the fit, against 64 in the Central region;
with so few stations to compare, the data cannot separate distance from attractiveness
there. Those two estimates should not be interpreted.

**The regional model predicts held-out stations better.** Its cross-validated R² is
`r round(m_of("R5", "R2_log"), 2)` against `r round(m_of("M3", "R2_log"), 2)`, its typical error
falls from `r round(m_of("M3", "MdAPE_pct"))`% to `r round(m_of("R5", "MdAPE_pct"))`%, and its
bias in the total falls from `r round(m_of("M3", "bias_pct"))`% to
`r round(m_of("R5", "bias_pct"))`%. It reduces the clustering of the errors (Moran's I from
`r round(cal$moran_resid$estimate[1], 2)` to `r round(va$moran_r5$estimate[1], 2)`) without removing
it, which fits the view that unseen private housing is the larger cause. Exponential decay
does worse than the power form (`r round(m_of("EXP", "R2_log"), 2)`).

**Do the predictions change?** The JRL runs through the West, where the regional exponent
is much steeper than the island-wide one, so I re-ran the expanded network with R5
(`R/07_scenario_r5.R`). The ranking of the 29 new stations barely moves (rank correlation
`r round(r5$summ$rho_new, 2)`); total JRL boardings change by `r pct(r5$summ$ratio_new_jrl - 1)`
and CRL boardings by `r pct(r5$summ$ratio_new_crl - 1)`; the changes at existing stations rank
almost identically (`r round(r5$summ$rho_change, 2)`). The one material difference is at the
western interchanges: Jurong East's modelled loss grows from
`r pct(-r5$cmp$change_pct[r5$cmp$name == "Jurong East"])` to
`r pct(-r5$cmp$change_pct_r5[r5$cmp$name == "Jurong East"])` and Boon Lay's from
`r pct(-r5$cmp$change_pct[r5$cmp$name == "Boon Lay"])` to
`r pct(-r5$cmp$change_pct_r5[r5$cmp$name == "Boon Lay"])`, because with a steeper decay western
residents switch more readily to a nearer JRL station.

So the extension does two things. It shows that the effect of distance on station choice
varies across Singapore in a way that can be measured and plausibly interpreted, and it
shows that the main conclusions do not depend on assuming one value everywhere, except at
the western interchanges, where the regional model is the better guide.

```{r code-06}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "R/06_value_added.R and R/07_scenario_r5.R: regional distance decay"
#| code: !expr c(readLines("R/06_value_added.R"), "", readLines("R/07_scenario_r5.R"))
```

# Uncertainty and sensitivity

## What the intervals cover, and what they do not

The intervals in @fig-params and @fig-new come from refitting the model 200 times, each
time on a random resample of the fitted stations. They show how much the estimates would
move with a somewhat different set of stations. They are **not** a range for the number of
people who will actually use a station. They cover:

- uncertainty in the estimated exponents and $k$ (parameter uncertainty).

They do not cover:

- whether the model's form is right (specification uncertainty; section 8 and @tbl-sens
  give a sense of it);
- the scatter of individual stations around the model, which is large (a typical miss of a
  third, section 6.1);
- spatial error, such as the clustering of misses (section 6.3);
- changes in homes, jobs and surroundings before the stations open;
- which stations actually open, and when (section 7.1).

## How much the results depend on my choices

```{r tbl-sens}
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity of the fitted model and the new-station predictions to two choices: the exclusion threshold and the radius of the choice set. Accuracy is cross-validated. The last two columns compare each variant's predictions for the 29 new stations with the main model's."
sens$sens |>
  transmute(Variant = variant, `Stations fitted` = n_fit, `Distance exponent` = round(lambda, 2),
            `Lines served` = round(n_lines, 2), `R² on the 148 main stations` = round(common_R2_log, 2),
            `New-station total vs main` = pct(new_total_vs_main - 1),
            `New-station rank correlation` = round(new_rank_rho, 2)) |>
  mutate(`New-station total vs main` = ifelse(Variant == "min 1000 DU within 1 km", "main model", `New-station total vs main`)) |>
  kable()
```

**The exclusion rule.** Thresholds of 500 or 2,000 dwelling units give almost the same
model and the same new-station ranking. Removing the rule entirely makes the model fit
`r sens$sens$n_fit[1]` stations, including private-estate, central and industrial ones that
HDB homes cannot explain; it then has to stretch the distance effect to cover them (the
exponent flattens to `r round(sens$sens$lambda[1], 2)`), and its accuracy on the residential
stations falls from `r round(sens$sens$common_R2_log[3], 2)` to
`r round(sens$sens$common_R2_log[1], 2)`. Excluding those stations is therefore not a way of
hiding errors; it keeps the model to the stations its data can explain. The price is that
the model says nothing reliable about stations whose riders are workers, students or
travellers. Under the main model, the excluded stations receive a median of
`r pct(median(sens$excluded$ratio))` of their observed boardings, and the four Tuas stations,
beyond the reach of any HDB block, receive none.

**The choice-set radius.** A 2 km radius fits worse and a 5 km radius fits better
(`r round(sens$sens$common_R2_log[6], 2)` against `r round(sens$sens$common_R2_log[3], 2)`), with
almost the same new-station predictions. I kept the 3 km set because it was chosen before
seeing any results; switching to whichever radius scores best on the test stations would
make the reported accuracy look better than it really is.


# What this means for rail planning

The model gives a defensible estimate of one part of a station's demand: morning
boardings by people living in HDB flats nearby. Four lessons follow, each with what the
model supports, what it only suggests, and what evidence is still missing.

**Residential demand.** The model supports a ranking of the new stations by how many HDB
residents they would draw in the morning, with Tengah Plantation, Serangoon North, Pasir
Ris East and Choa Chu Kang West at the top. It suggests these stations would be among the
busier morning boarding points from the day they open. It does not establish their actual
ridership, which also depends on private housing, new blocks and travel habits; ridership
at comparable new stations after opening would be the evidence to look for.

**Employment and institutional demand.** Aviation Park, Jurong Pier, Jurong Hill, Loyang,
the Nanyang stations and Tukang draw few HDB residents. The model supports only that. It
does not support delaying their opening: their purpose is to bring people to jobs, the
university and the airport, which needs a model of where people go in the morning, using
employment and student numbers and the origin-destination data that could not be obtained
here.

**Redistribution at existing stations.** The model supports that the new lines would move
a large share of morning boardings away from Chinese Garden, Lakeside, Pioneer, Bukit
Batok and Kovan, and towards the new CRL interchanges. It suggests that station entries,
platforms and access routes at those stations would carry fewer HDB residents. It does
not establish changes in train crowding, which depend on transfers and train capacity, or
what should happen to feeder bus routes, which would need a bus-network analysis.

**Further validation.** Before these numbers inform an operational decision, the model
should be tested against a real opening (fitted before a station opens, checked after),
extended to private housing, and given travel distances along the walking network instead
of straight lines. The regional model (section 8) is the better choice where distance
matters most, in the West and North-East.

# Limitations

- **Only HDB homes.** Private housing, about one resident in five, is invisible to the
  model. This is the most likely reason for the clustered errors at city-fringe stations.
- **Only morning boardings from home.** Total daily ridership, and demand from workers,
  students and travellers, is outside the model.
- **Straight-line distance** stands in for the actual walk or bus ride.
- **Today's homes and surroundings.** New housing, and new shops and services around new
  stations, are not included; predictions for stations in developing areas could move in
  either direction.
- **Fixed total demand.** Adding stations only redistributes boardings; it cannot capture
  people who start using the train because a station opened near them.
- **No test against a real opening.** The cross-validation hides mature stations, not new
  ones.
- **Three months** of data from one year.

# Reproducing this analysis

The analysis runs as a chain of R scripts. Each writes its results to `data/derived/`,
and this report and the slides only read those results. If they are missing, rendering
this page runs the whole chain first (see the setup chunk).

| Step | Script | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `R/00_config.R`, `R/00_download.R` | every setting in one place; fetches the input data |
| 1 | `R/01_street_codes.R` | links HDB dwelling units to block outlines (OneMap) |
| 2 | `R/02_osm_poi.R` | points of interest and bus stops from OpenStreetMap |
| 3 | `R/prep_functions.R`, `R/03_prepare.R` | origins, stations, attraction variables, the two data frames |
| 4 | `R/04_calibrate.R`, `R/04b_diagnostics.R` | calibration, validation, bootstrap, checks |
| 5 | `R/05_scenario.R`, `R/05b_phased_scenarios.R` | the expanded networks |
| 6 | `R/06_value_added.R`, `R/07_scenario_r5.R` | regional distance decay |
| 7 | `R/08_sensitivity.R` | model comparison and sensitivity |

: The analysis pipeline. Run from `Take-home_Ex/Take-home_Ex03/`; `README.md` gives the commands. {#tbl-pipeline}

Random numbers are seeded (`SEED = 626` in `R/00_config.R`). The raw data are not stored in
the repository; `R/00_download.R` fetches them, and `README.md` explains the two steps that
need a person (an LTA DataMall API key, and one LTA file saved from a browser).

```{r session}
#| code-summary: "Software versions"
pk <- c("sf", "dplyr", "tidyr", "ggplot2", "MCI", "spdep", "httr2", "patchwork", "ggrepel", "ragg", "knitr")
tibble(package = c("R", pk), version = c(paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = "."),
                                          map_chr(pk, \(p) as.character(packageVersion(p))))) |>
  kable()
```
